key_points: The editor's "Between Ourselves" explains why the Armed Forces Special Powers Act cover feature is placed later in the issue so readers weigh the civil-liberties question themselves, and introduces Tagore-anniversary material and memorial pieces on M. S. Gore, Shyam Chainani and Kancherla Rama Rao.

Reader letters press Freedom First to focus on corruption, police reform and CBI independence, with one correspondent invoking Tunisia's mass protests and another warning that proposed Direct Tax Code procedures will multiply harassment and corruption at tax offices.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Thank God for Pakistan!" contrasts India's corruption and bureaucratic failure with Pakistan's deeper crisis of religious radicalisation after the murder of Governor Salman Taseer, arguing India's free press and plural public sphere remain valuable despite its flaws.

Ashok Karnik's "Corporate Ethics" examines the Niira Radia tapes as a study in lobbying and media influence, accepting legitimate policy advocacy as part of democracy while calling for legislation to regulate lobbying and questioning whether enforcement agencies acted coherently.

Cyrus Guzder's tribute "Shyam Chainani - Unflinching Warrior for the Environment" reviews Chainani's book Heritage and the Environment, presenting him as an incorruptible, persistent campaigner on Bombay planning, coastal regulation and heritage law.

J. S. Apte's biographical tribute to M. S. Gore traces his career at the Tata Institute of Social Sciences and stresses his moderation and independence during the Emergency, including his refusal to sign a statement attacking Jayaprakash Narayan.

Sharad Joshi's "The Rural Perspective: Understanding Onion Politics" argues that export bans and panic responses to onion price rises harm farmers, contrasting the 1980 episode with 2010-11 and opposing blanket bans as damaging to long-term export credibility.

In his pre-budget note to the Finance Minister, Joshi cites NCRB data on 17,368 farmer suicides in 2009 and criticises the Debt Relief and Loan Waivers Scheme, weak seed and biofuel policy, and prejudice against futures markets, defending futures as a legitimate marketing channel.

Ashok Karnik's Point Counter Point weighs Wen Jiabao's India visit, Rahul Gandhi's leaked remark on Hindu terrorism, and the demand for a Joint Parliamentary Committee on corruption, arguing a JPC may achieve little unless the wider culture of impunity changes.

S. V. Raju's editorial asks whether Freedom First needs a new paradigm amid deteriorating governance, defining the magazine's goal as building a liberal society with a liberal temper and warning against accepting institutional erosion as inevitable.

B. Ramesh Babu's cover essay "The Second Liberation of Egypt" reads the 2011 uprising as a second liberation after Nasser's era, praises the disciplined protestors in Tahrir Square, and contrasts Egypt's military restraint with Tiananmen Square while warning that toppling a dictator is not enough without democratic institutions.

The open letter "On 'Deficit Governance': An Open Letter from some concerned Citizens," signed by prominent figures from business, economics, law and public life, calls for independent regulatory bodies and empowered Lok Ayuktas, linking good governance to poverty alleviation and growth.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Congress Party On Suicide Watch" argues the Congress party's half-hearted response to scandals - the Commonwealth Games affair, Suresh Kalmadi, the cabinet reshuffle, A. Raja, foreign black money and P. J. Thomas - is destroying its own credibility.

The editorial recalls the magazine's earlier anti-communist and pro-market educational work while identifying rapidly worsening governance, stagnating reforms and crony capitalism as the present, more urgent problem.

The issue's table of contents also lists later pieces on development, environmental impact assessments, the Graham Staines judgment and Rabindranath Tagore, though these fall outside the rendered pages and are not digested here.

S. V. Raju's editorial acknowledges the Fukushima disaster and expresses sympathy for Japan, explaining why Freedom First is still publishing planned articles on the Jaitapur Nuclear Power Project and calling for dispassionate liberal debate on nuclear energy.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Do Indians Have the Stomach for a People's Revolution" uses Egypt's uprising as a mirror for India, arguing Indian democracy has been manipulated by rulers through inherited colonial habits of secrecy and patronage, while crediting the RTI Act and media scrutiny as partial signs of change.
N. Vittal's "Issues In Governance" continues the issue's public-accountability theme, situated within the magazine's ongoing cluster of essays on corruption and institutional reform.

Bal Phondke's "The Controversy is a Smoke Screen" argues opposition to the Jaitapur nuclear project is overstated, describing India's three-stage nuclear programme and thorium ambitions and responding to Chernobyl- and Fukushima-type fears by citing France's and Japan's heavy reliance on nuclear power.
The editorial notes that no reader responded to the March issue's question of whether India should seek superpower status or focus on poverty, health, education and infrastructure.
The issue's table of contents also turns to religion, blasphemy, the Union Budget, nuclear disarmament and book reviews, though these lie beyond the rendered chunk.

S. V. Raju's editorial frames the Anna Hazare movement as a test case for liberals, balancing anti-corruption urgency against concern for constitutional democracy and arguing that democracy is not exhausted by elections.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Hazar Voices for Anna" takes a skeptical view of the Hazare agitation, doubting whether a Lokpal bill can cleanse governance and arguing politicians are unlikely to pass laws that seriously threaten themselves.

Ranga Rao DS's "The IAC or India Against Corruption Movement" addresses the institutional meaning of the campaign as part of the issue's cover-feature cluster on Anna Hazare and participatory democracy.
Ashok Karnik's Point Counter Point continues the magazine's recurring format of weighing multiple sides of current public issues, appearing after the anti-corruption cover feature.
D. R. Pendse's "India Wins World Cup 2011" marks India's cricket World Cup victory as a cultural and current-affairs item under the Changing Times section.

The cover feature as a whole gathers several voluntary contributions on Anna Hazare, India Against Corruption, the Jan Lokpal and citizen mobilisation, framed by the editor as revealing the difficulty of being a liberal amid hope and constitutional caution.

The editorial frames Osama bin Laden's killing as an occasion to examine terrorism and state capacity, asking readers not to join processions celebrating a terrorist's memory and contrasting the American operation with India's failure to act against Dawood Ibrahim.

Ashok Karnik's "Operation Geronimo" treats the bin Laden raid as a strategic and political operation rather than mere revenge, emphasising its symbolic value in demonstrating that long-delayed accountability can still arrive.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Can India Pull Off An Osama To Get Dawood?" argues the obstacle to capturing Dawood Ibrahim, tied to the 1993 Bombay bomb blasts, is political will and state resolve rather than operational capacity.

Era Sezhiyan's "The Shah Commission Report Lost, and Regained" recounts how this record of Emergency-era abuses was lost and recovered, framing its archival recovery as part of democratic accountability.
P. M. Kamath's "Hazare Must Plan for Evolutionary Changes!" argues Anna Hazare's anti-corruption movement needs durable institutional reform rather than reliance on agitation alone.
The editorial also marks June as the anniversary month of the Emergency and notes Tamil Nadu's election results and a tribute to Nausheryan Framji Suntook.

S. V. Raju's editorial contrasts India's history of one-party dominance, the Emergency, the Janata interlude and coalition politics with the present tension between government and civil society, arguing civil society should strengthen rather than confront Parliament.

The cover feature "The Recent Elections to Five State Assemblies: Some Perspectives" argues that local issues and regional political cultures, rather than a uniform national ideology, shaped the results, citing Kerala's volatility and Tamil Nadu's distinct electoral logic.

Ashok Karnik's Point Counter Point criticises the government's handling of Baba Ramdev's anti-corruption fast and reads the Karachi naval-base attack as evidence of danger inside Pakistan while cautioning against reckless interpretation of its instability.

Sharad Bailur's "The Lokpal and What It Entails" warns against ceding large constitutional power to unelected civil society representatives, proposing instead performance-linked appointments, recall of representatives and transparent political finance.

H. R. Bapu Satyanarayana's "For Whom the Bell Tolls" links public anger over Anna Hazare and Baba Ramdev to the government's reluctance to address black money and to the CVC appointment, 2G, CWG and Kanimozhi controversies.
The editorial warns that the Lokpal confrontation risks becoming a collision course between civil society and Parliament even as it welcomes signs of anti-corruption energy.

The editorial dedicates the issue to P. V. Narasimha Rao as "the real liberator of the Indian economy," crediting him with enabling Manmohan Singh's reforms while criticising the Congress dynasty's renewed control on India's 65th year of independence.

V. Balachandran's "Why is India Not Protected from Terrorist Attacks?" argues India's counterterrorism policy repeatedly cycles through grief, blame of Pakistan and forgotten reforms, contrasting this with the post-9/11 United States' Joint Terrorism Task Force model.

M. D. Kini's "The Citizen Vs. The State or The Citizen and the State" defends citizen action through PIL, RTI and the proposed Lokpal, arguing the 2G, CWG and Adarsh scams were exposed by citizens and courts rather than state institutions.

D. S. Ranga Rao's "A Providential Intervention by Anna Hazare" replies to Sharad Bailur's July critique, arguing unelected civil-society bodies already operate within government, such as the National Advisory Council, and defending the Lokpal as an accountability mechanism.
Ashok Karnik's Point Counter Point continues the magazine's recurring format, following the issue's rural-perspective article and preceding material on the May 2011 elections.
The editorial criticises dynastic control over the Indian state and asks why Manmohan Singh did not resign when politically constrained.

The editorial explains the issue was delayed by the question of whether liberals should back Anna Hazare's Jan Lokpal or the government's weaker bill, worrying about confrontation between Parliament and civil society while recognising ordinary citizens' attraction to Hazare.

D. S. Ranga Rao's "Two Lokpal Bills: Which is Better? Depends on Who's Asking" compares the competing drafts and argues that judgments about the better bill depend on the standpoint of the person asking.
Sharad Bailur's "Active Citizenship, Democracy and Anna Hazare" examines whether citizen action strengthens democratic accountability or slips into pressure politics.
Ashok Karnik's "Terror Returns" addresses renewed terrorist violence, broadening the issue's agenda beyond the Lokpal debate to national security.
The cover pairs Hazare's Ram Lila rally with an older image of Jayaprakash Narayan addressing crowds in 1975, explicitly linking the moment to earlier mass politics.

The issue's table of contents also lists pieces on India's social divisions, religious politics, water strategy and fake encounter killings, alongside T. J. S. George on JP's India and Rabindranath Tagore's Atma-Parichaya, though most fall beyond the rendered pages.

The editorial compares the Anna Hazare movement to Jayaprakash Narayan's Total Revolution as history's largest field agitation, and argues liberals should respect Parliament as "democracy's temple" and let the Standing Committee do its work on the Lokpal drafts.
Jagdeep S. Chhokar's "Beyond Hazare" asks what comes after charismatic protest and how institutional reform can proceed once public agitation has forced anti-corruption onto the national agenda.

Sharad Bailur's "Corruption or An Attempt to Destroy Democracy?" continues his skeptical liberal line, questioning whether anti-corruption agitation risks undermining constitutional balance and procedure.
Firoze Hirjikaka's "Anna's Revolution - Cause and Aftermath" reflects on the public causes behind the Hazare movement and what may follow the fast and its parliamentary referral.
J. S. Apte's article on the declining child sex ratio in Maharashtra shifts the issue from corruption politics to gendered social reform and demographic imbalance.
The editor credits Hazare with waking a "somnolent people" and invigorating democracy even while urging patience for the Standing Committee process over street pressure.
The editorial reports strong reader appreciation for the October anti-corruption issue but explains the magazine will defer further Lokpal analysis until the parliamentary Standing Committee reports.

Sharad Bailur's "Rectitude and Paralysis of Governance" argues good intentions and institutional caution can themselves produce governance paralysis, warning that excessive caution can disable public administration.
Vasant G. Gandhi's article discusses India's interest-rate hikes as a response to inflation, raising the growth-inflation tradeoff facing monetary policy.

D. B. Shekatkar's "Terrorism as Extension of Foreign Policy" frames terrorism as a tool used in pursuit of state and strategic objectives, expanding the issue's scope from governance to national security.

The issue also carries Neelakant Patri on wealth, Ashok Karnik's Point Counter Point, Furdoon S. B. Mehta arguing the Army needs its own voice, and the opening of Firoze Hirjikaka's article on Narendra Modi.
The editor also reflects on reader discomfort with serious articles and comments on political vindictiveness and coalition weakness.

The editorial gives pride of place to Subhash C. Kashyap's note on Standing Committees, arguing India's parliamentary system has survived despite being "mauled" by Congress-led governments, and notes Anna Hazare sought passage through Parliament rather than another constitutional amendment.

Subhash C. Kashyap's "The Standing Committees of Parliament" explains the committee mechanism now relevant to the Lokpal process, reinforcing that legislative scrutiny is part of democratic procedure rather than evasion of public accountability.
Sheryar Ookerjee's "India's Growing Leadership Deficit" addresses the shortage of credible leadership in Indian public life, linking political weakness to governance problems.

Sharad Joshi's rural-perspective article on the National Land Acquisition and Rehabilitation and Resettlement Bill, 2011, places property, rural rights and state acquisition powers within the wider governance debate.
The editorial also reports Quest's recognition and the publication of Minoo Masani's lecture "Of Four Real Leaders."
The issue's table of contents lists later pieces on the Indo-Pak wars, Vijay Mallya, Rajagopalachari, the Valmiki Ramayana and book reviews beyond the rendered range.

The editorial recalls the Second Five Year Plan's role in India's near-pauperisation and traces the Swatantra Party's 1960 call for a grievance-hearing authority as an anticipation of the Ombudsman/Lokpal idea, crediting Narasimha Rao with helping India escape one economic disaster.
Sunil S. Bhandare's "The Fiscal Drift: 2011-12" opens the issue's economic-policy cluster, raising concerns about public finance discipline and state spending.

Sharu S. Rangnekar's "Capitalism in Crisis" considers anxieties around capitalism after global economic turbulence, pairing a liberal defence of markets with concern for governance and fiscal responsibility.
Sharad Joshi's rural-perspective article on the Food Security Bill, 2011 brings farmers' and rural-economy concerns into the issue's debate over state intervention and entitlement policy.
The editorial criticises both the ruling coalition and the opposition for putting party interest above national interest amid parliamentary paralysis.

The issue also includes H. R. Bapu Satyanarayana on the Licence Permit Raj's "new avatar," K. K. Pathak on parties without politics, Ashok Karnik's Point Counter Point, and Sharad Bailur arguing for abolishing driving licences.

The editorial says the Anna Hazare movement went "from a bang to a whimper" after the Bombay fast exposed the campaign's limits, criticising Congress's dynastic politics while insisting corruption and the Lokpal remain central to public life.
Sunil S. Bhandare's pre-budget essay "Recharging Growth Strategy - Fiscal Challenges" looks ahead to the Union Budget and the fiscal pressures facing India's growth strategy.
Ashok Karnik's "The Lokpal Fiasco" treats the stalled Lokpal process as a disappointment after months of high public expectation.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Is Team Anna Losing Its Lustre?" questions whether the campaign's moral authority and public appeal are fading, treating the movement's credibility as distinct from the corruption issue itself.
R. C. Saxena's article raises further disquieting aspects of the Hazare movement, continuing the issue's critical reassessment of Team Anna after its momentum slowed.
The editor also notes the issue's Ramanujan tribute on the cover and introduces a new Adult Education feature.

The editorial contrasts the silence around Anna Hazare with routine election inducements and low civic participation, warning that institutional independence - of the judiciary, Election Commission and Army - remains vulnerable to partisan pressure.
Sunil S. Bhandare's article on monetary easing asks whether growth can be recharged through easier monetary policy, continuing the magazine's pre-budget and macroeconomic coverage.
T. H. Chowdary's "Is It Desirable to Stop Migration of Workers?" brings labour mobility and urban-rural economic questions into the issue.
Furdoon S. B. Mehta argues for the "Need for the Chief of Defence Staff in India," treating defence coordination as a governance problem.

The issue's table of contents also lists articles on Republic Day without public participation, political money, and the Indian Peace Keeping Force, alongside later material on Vivekananda, Almora and worker communism.
The editorial frames the whole issue around democratic decay persisting despite middle-class anti-corruption rhetoric.

The editorial reads recent Uttar Pradesh election results as evidence that voters get the governments they deserve, criticising UPA2's budget direction and warning about a return to licence-permit-quota habits.
B. Raman's article introduces the Lakhar movement in Tibet, grounding the cover's Tibetan flag in a political and cultural assertion of Tibetan nationhood.
Sunil S. Bhandare argues for external stability as a condition for recharging India's growth, treating macroeconomic and investor confidence as a policy concern.
K. K. Pathak's "The Genesis of Corruption: An Historical Perspective" treats corruption as a long-running institutional and social problem rather than only a current scandal.
The issue's table of contents also lists Firoze Hirjikaka on "the death of democracy" and later material on Putin, Dickens, Rukmini Devi and Indian cultural institutions.
The cover foregrounds the Lakhar movement in Tibet alongside the editorial's reflections on Mumbai municipal politics.

The editorial asks readers to move from diagnosis to remedies for corruption and misgovernance, summarising a four-front anti-corruption strategy of moral education, raising the cost of corruption, electoral reform and reducing opportunities for it, while criticising the 2012-13 budget's GAAR and retrospective tax provisions.
K. K. Pathak's "Explosive Times" responds to the turbulent political and policy climate described in the editorial.
Era Sezhiyan's "The Writing on the Wall" reads visible warning signs in contemporary politics and public life.
Suresh C. Sharma's Kargil War article opens the issue's Military Matters section, pairing with a further piece on General V. K. Singh and military controversy.
The editorial also references a paper by Subhash Athale and Harihar Khumbhojkar on national peril, corruption and the criminalisation of politics and bureaucracy.
The issue also covers D. R. Pendse's alarm over the 2012-13 Union Budget and the political drama around Dinesh Trivedi's resignation.

Firoze Hirjikaka's anniversary essay "Freedom First Senior Citizen" celebrates the magazine's sixty years on slender resources, loyal readers and unpaid articles, crediting Minoo Masani's founding vision.

S. V. Raju's "Introspection - 60 years On" places the milestone alongside the earlier 50-year compendium and 500th issue, quotes the magazine's first June 1952 article on the open society, and explains that digitisation, not another compendium, will preserve the archive.
Ashok Karnik's "The NCTC - An Assault on Federalism?" examines the National Counter Terrorism Centre's implications for the institutional balance between Centre and states.
The issue also moves into nature writing, social critique, drought, regionalism, hostages and Sachin Tendulkar's nomination as a Rajya Sabha MP.
The cover announces "60 years of standing by freedom," and the issue notes the archive's digitisation project and a forthcoming Freedom First web page.

The editorial marks Freedom First's resumption after its sixtieth anniversary, contrasting the collapse or compromise of international communist movements with India's still-unfinished task of building an honest open society, and announces the magazine's launch online at freedomfirst.in.
Sunil Bhandare's "A Ritualistic Call for Austerity!" critiques calls for austerity as often ritualistic rather than serious fiscal policy.
N. Vittal's "A Pragmatic Approach to Clean up India" aligns with the magazine's anti-corruption and governance concerns, though only its opening is rendered.
The issue's table of contents also lists pieces on monsoon forecasting, the presidential election, Ashok Karnik's Point Counter Point, and a discussion of Maulana Azad's India Wins Freedom.
Later material on foreign relations, China and the environment is listed in the contents but falls outside the rendered pages.

The editorial notes a redesigned inside front page listing the advisory board and editorial team, Tina D'Souza's retirement, Kashmira Rao's new role, and the expected election of a senior Congress figure as President while acknowledging P. A. Sangma's contest.
Bal Phondke's "The Eighteenth Camel" leads the issue and gives the cover its title, likely using the eighteenth-camel parable as a frame for public reasoning.
Rca Godole's article comments on the Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel's report, bringing environmental and expert-policy questions into an issue otherwise focused on science, defence and strategy.
Nitin G. Raut's "Agni V - A Good Defensive Shield" treats India's missile capability as a strategic defensive asset tied to the issue's cover imagery.
B. Ramesh Babu's "India as a Global Player: Power and Purpose" examines power and purpose in India's foreign policy.
The issue's table of contents also lists pieces on corruption as a service industry, Indian proverbs, the Lal Masjid, Dr. Kotnis and book reviews beyond the rendered chunk.

The issue is led by the August 11 Mumbai/Azad Maidan riot; the cover asks whether there was "a riot without reason," quoting newspaper accounts of mob violence against police and vehicles, with the editor sensing the state failed to reassure citizens.

Ashok Karnik's "A Riot without Reason?" is the central cover article addressing the disorder, following the editor's eyewitness-style account of chaos, rumours and the state's failure to reassure the public.
Govind Keshav Bhide's article on "Avoiding Power Grid Trips" argues for solar energy as an imperative response to electricity reliability and national grid infrastructure concerns.
Ranga Kota's article examines India's Olympic performance and what it reveals about the country's sporting capability.

The issue's table of contents also lists a nature column on Madhavaiah Krishnan, Point Counter Point, an agricultural essay, and later reflections on Independence Day, chief ministers, Rousseau and secularism.

The issue memorialises Verghese Kurien on the cover as "the right man at the right place and time," while the editorial supports the Prime Minister's resumption of economic reforms and defends the diesel price hike as a partial recognition that broad subsidies damage the economy.
Sharad Bailur's "Untold Tales of Verghese Kurien" presents Kurien as a significant institution-builder, tying the memorial focus to the milk-themed cover.
Sunil Bhandare's "The State of the Economy" follows the editorial's defence of reforms, diesel price rationalisation and subsidy restraint.
Nitin G. Raut revisits "The Mumbai Riots of August 11, 2012," continuing the previous issue's concern with public disorder, policing and communal politics.
The editorial insists that corruption and scams still need rigorous prosecution even as it supports the reform push.
The issue's table of contents also lists later pieces on China, the 1965 war, Allan Octavian Hume and a book on birds.

The issue honours Malala Yousafzai on the cover as a 15-year-old example of courage against religious fanaticism, while the editorial revisits Mumbai police handling of the Azad Maidan riot aftermath and asks whether vote-bank politics shaped the official response.
Sunil S. Bhandare's "Much Ado about New Policy Reforms" discusses the reception of new policy reforms within the magazine's economic-policy frame.
H. R. Bapu Satyanarayana's "The State of the Nation Today" offers a broad political diagnosis of India in late 2012.
R. Srinivasan's profile "A. Madhaviah (1872-1925)" continues the magazine's Profiles of Indian Liberals column, highlighting a historical liberal figure amid the issue's current-affairs focus.
The issue's table of contents also lists a nature encounter with tigers, Point Counter Point, and the opening of P. M. Kamath's piece on Brajesh Mishra.
Later pieces on China, Patel, subsidies, federalisation and the Madras High Court are listed in the contents but fall outside the rendered pages.

The cover honours Major Shaitan Singh and the soldiers he led as a "forgotten tale of heroism," while the editorial clarifies that the magazine's liberal position means judgment from a liberal perspective rather than dogma, using FDI as an example of contextual reasoning.
Sunil S. Bhandare's "Ease of Doing Business - India's Dismal Ranking!" frames economic reform through India's poor regulatory-performance ranking.
Suresh C. Sharma's article on FDI in organised retail trade takes up the editorial's example of liberal support for free markets tempered by Indian context.
N. S. Venkataraman argues in "India's Anti-Corruption Movement Now Derailed" that the Anna Hazare-Lokpal campaign has lost its way, continuing the magazine's long-running governance-reform coverage.
The issue's table of contents also lists pieces on Bt brinjal, India-Japan relations, Shaitan Singh, Rajaji and ancient navigation.

The cover montage "India 2012" and its editorial link the Delhi bus gang-rape of a young medical student with Narendra Modi's return to power in Gujarat, criticising theatrical television coverage of the rape case while arguing Modi's victory forced even critics to acknowledge Gujarat's governance record.
Manohar Parrikar's "Effective Governance in a Federal Polity" argues from the standpoint of state-level administration for practical governance over symbolic politics.
Sunil S. Bhandare's "The Employment-Unemployment Conundrum" places labour-market distress within the magazine's recurring concern with growth and reform.
Kashinath A. Divecha's "Industrial Chaos" examines disorder in industry and labour relations as an economic and governance cost.
Aroon Tikekar's "Bal Thackeray: The Only Thackeray!" begins a political appraisal of Thackeray after his death, though only its opening page is rendered.
The issue's table of contents also lists later material on press freedom, foreign relations, C. Rajagopalachari and Minoo Masani.

The issue is explicitly dedicated to the memory of Nirbhaya; its editorial responds to the Delhi assault and killing, the spontaneous protests around Parliament and Rashtrapati Bhavan, and the state's water-cannon response, contrasting this outrage with organised anti-corruption mobilisation.
Kusum Chopra's "The Delhi Gang Rape Case: Rapes and Apes" addresses the case directly, framing sexual violence as a broader civic and moral failure.
H. R. Bapu Satyanarayana's "The Gruesome Assault" records the brutality of the Nirbhaya case and the public demand for justice and safety.
Firoze Hirjikaka's "No Lessons Learnt" argues authorities and society have repeatedly failed to learn from breakdowns of public order and women's safety.
Y. Sivaji's "Advocating the Farmers' Interest" shifts the issue toward economic policy, placing agricultural concerns within the magazine's broader liberal debate.
Sunil S. Bhandare's "The Twelfth Five Year Plan" assesses national planning through the lens of economic priorities and policy realism.
Kashinath Divecha's "Industrial Chaos - II" continues the previous issue's discussion of industrial disorder as a governance and economic problem.

The cover uses Aadhaar/UID as its theme, calling it "a step in the right direction"; the editorial turns first to the Afzal Guru hanging, arguing rule of law and firm governance matter most while questioning both capital punishment and the secrecy around the execution.

Sharad Bailur's lead article "Aadhar: Good or Bad?" frames the scheme as a liberal-democratic compromise between state capacity, privacy and safeguards, arguing power ceded to the state must remain limited and accountable.

Sunil S. Bhandare's "The Twelfth Five Year Plan - 2" focuses on financing, falling GDP growth, budgetary constraints and the need to shift more development responsibility to states and local authorities.

P. Koshy's "Retail Revolution, FDI and the Meaning of Reforms" argues reform should not be defined only by subsidy withdrawal and foreign investment, but must also create a fair operating climate for MSMEs and informal enterprises.
The issue's table of contents also lists pieces on the need for a change in male attitudes, Pakistan's "Barbaric Act," and a comparison of the Congress conclave with the Chinese Congress.
Later pieces on Pakistan, minorities, Aruna Shanbaug, armed forces unrest and Bernard Levin are listed in the contents but fall outside the rendered chunk.

The issue criticises Budget 2013-14 as a letdown and "an exercise in denial"; the editorial portrays Indian politics as dominated by survival strategies and capitulation to vote-bank pressures, while also discussing the anti-rape law, Italian marines, and the launch of the Children First Party of India.
M. R. Venkatesh's "Budget 2013 - An Elaborate Exercise in Denial" criticises stalled projects, policy paralysis, and the handling of the Food Security Act allocation.
Sunil S. Bhandare's "Twelfth Plan and the 2013-14 Union Budget - 3" questions the feasibility of a large increase in plan expenditure given fiscal constraints and implementation capacity.

Nitin G. Raut's "The New Delhi Protest" describes the public reaction to Nirbhaya's rape and death as spontaneous youth anger against lawlessness and unaccountable power, comparing it to Tahrir, Bastille, Tiananmen and Nav Nirman.

Suresh Sharma's article on the Justice Verma Committee Report defends court-martials against blanket civilian-court treatment while examining recommendations on armed-forces accountability for sexual violence.
The issue's table of contents also lists later pieces on terrorism, the NCTC and the Children First Party, outside the rendered range.

The cover places Margaret Thatcher on the cover as "the Iron Lady"; the editorial combines concern about another child rape case in Delhi with a tribute to Thatcher's clarity and governance, arguing India lacks similar qualities in public life.

S. V. Raju's Thatcher memorial, "Remembering Margaret Thatcher - The Iron Lady," reprints Freedom First's own 1979 response to her election alongside a 1983 Minoo Masani note praising her privatisation and anti-Soviet resolve.
Rca Godbole's "Patenting in India" discusses intellectual property policy, linking innovation and law to national development.

Arvind Ilamaran's "New Line of Enquiry: FDI in India" argues foreign-investment debates are trapped in political narratives and fear of foreign entrants, treating FDI as an unavoidable phase in India's development while calling for better scrutiny of consequences.
Ranga Kota's "Beyond Budgets" moves from budget arithmetic to larger questions of governance and policy implementation.
The issue also carries an in memoriam note for Major General Eustace D'Souza and pieces on the Boston bombing, outside the fully digested portion.

The cover line "The Descent Continues" frames an editorial recalling the magazine's 1993 coverage of communal violence and the Bombay bomb blasts, connecting Dawood Ibrahim, cricket spot-fixing and public scandal to a broader collapse of moral fibre in Indian public life.

Sunil S. Bhandare's "The Twelfth Plan and Industry - Issues and Challenges (4)" contrasts India's stagnant manufacturing share with stronger Asian performance, arguing implementation and investor confidence are central to industrial revival.

Sharad Joshi's "Why We Must Boycott Chinese Goods" calls for an economic boycott after Chinese incursions, linking border security, Tibet and Pakistan to a consumer-protest strategy tied to Swatantra Bharat Paksha.

B. Ramesh Babu's "China Does It Again: Retreat After Accomplishing the Mission" argues China gained strategically from its April-May 2013 Ladakh intrusion near Daulat Beg Oldie despite its apparent withdrawal, criticising India's confused and secretive response.
Suresh C. Sharma's "An Opportunity Lost" begins a reflection whose argument cannot be fully captured since only its opening page is rendered.
The issue's table of contents also lists pieces on constitutional status for the CBI, the Right to Education Act and sanitising legislatures, outside the rendered range.
From Darkness to Light is a Swatantra Party publication recovered from the CCS archive, attributed to the party's literature though its specific author is not legible from the scan.
The source is an image-only scan with no usable OCR text layer, so its arguments and contents cannot yet be summarized from the body text.
The record remains a bibliographic entry pending OCR and editorial review to establish its author, date and substantive content.
The PDF is linked in the archive for reference, and the work is provisionally classified under Swatantra Party literature, economic freedom and the agrarian economy.
Poshindyanchi Lokshahi ("The Democracy of the Providers") is a Marathi book by Sharad Joshi, the economist who founded the Shetkari Sanghatana farmers' movement in Maharashtra.

The title turns on Joshi's coinage poshinda - the one who nourishes or provides, meaning the farmer-producer - framing his recurring thesis that India's political economy is rigged against the rural producers who feed the nation.
The source is a scanned image without a usable text layer, so a substantive summary of the book's contents could not be extracted; the entry awaits OCR and editorial review.
The record is classified within the Sharad Joshi and Shetkari Sanghatana corpus, with the PDF linked for readers pending fuller cataloguing.
